issues.title: Squashing is specified over every RPC request, with no exclusion for RPCSEC_GSS
issues.author: chucklever
issues.body:
Drafted with AI assistance from a review pass; quotes and citations verified against the source documents.

-03 §3 specifies the credential replacement over every request on the session:

```
   The receiving system (an RPC server) then
   replaces the RPC user, as carried in the RPC header credential and
   verifier fields in each RPC request within the TLS session, with the
   user identity specified in the certificate used to authenticate that
   session.
```

§3.2 step 6 repeats it, and adds that the original credential is discarded:

```
   6.  For each incoming RPC request on this TLS session, replace the
       credential information in the RPC header with the identity
       extracted from the certificate.  The original credential
       information in the RPC header is ignored.
```

Nothing scopes the replacement to particular authentication flavors. "RPCSEC" appears nowhere in -03, and `git log -S RPCSEC` over the draft source returns no commit in any revision.

RFC 9289 §4.2.1 goes the other way for GSS sessions:

```
   Authentication of RPCSEC_GSS users is unchanged by the use of TLS.
```

SP4_MACH_CRED is defined over an RPCSEC_GSS machine credential, so a server that replaces that credential removes what the state protection is defined over. Rick Macklem raised the interaction on the nfsv4 list on 19 March 2024, together with a possible SP4_MACH_CRED_RPC to resolve it; neither has been carried into any revision. https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/nfsv4/BTubpDlJyAW0lkupFZPCyRV_RWg

State which authentication flavors squashing applies to. If AUTH_SYS and AUTH_NONE only, say so in §3, and say what a server does when an RPCSEC_GSS request arrives on a session whose certificate carries a squashing otherName.

comments.author: chucklever
comments.body:
Drafted with AI assistance under close review; RFC 2203 and RFC 5531 structures verified against the published text.

Rick's reply off-list (2026-08-21) says the FreeBSD implementation ignores all RPC credentials, RPCSEC_GSS included, and that he would accept an exception without arguing for one. His reservation is that the exception obscures the one-user-per-device model he built for.

Proposed rule: identity squashing applies to requests whose credential flavor is AUTH_NONE or AUTH_SYS. A request using RPCSEC_GSS is processed under the identity established by its GSS context. That resolves the SP4_MACH_CRED interaction above, since the machine credential survives the session and the state protection remains defined over something still present.

A certificate cannot carry an RPCSEC_GSS credential in any case. Section 5.1 of RFC 2203 defines it as gss_proc, seq_num, service, and a context handle; the principal is established during context creation and lives in server-side context state. The id-on-gssExportedName otherName carries a name rather than a credential, so the exclusion does not strand it.

That name form still earns its OID, under a use case -03 does not describe. Users hold Kerberos principals, the machine holds none, and the machine's credential is a bare AUTH_SYS uid 0 that no server should believe. The TLS certificate authenticates the machine and names a service account principal as the squash target, so the machine's non-GSS traffic executes as an identity the server already knows from its KDC and its ACLs, while its users' traffic continues under their own proven identities. This is the second paragraph of §1.2, a service running as a single assigned identity where the TGT lifetime does not fit the service lifetime, with the certificate supplying what a keytab would supply.

Two consequences for the text.

§7.3 is falsified by the rule:

```
   All RPC operations within a TLS session containing an identity
   squashing otherName execute under the same user identity.
```

A session under this rule carries the certificate identity for its non-GSS traffic and the GSS-established identity for the rest. Session Binding needs to bind the certificate identity to the former only.

§5's guidance for GSSExportedName becomes backwards:

```
   GSSExportedName  Suitable for environments using GSS-API mechanisms
      like Kerberos.  This format fits naturally into existing GSS-API
      deployments but requires that servers support the specific
      mechanism indicated by the nameType OID.
```

A session that uses RPCSEC_GSS is the one case where squashing does not apply. The entry should say the form suits a server that keys identities by principal, on sessions whose traffic is not RPCSEC_GSS.

Rick, does the FreeBSD server do anything today when an RPCSEC_GSS request arrives on a session whose certificate carries a squashing otherName?

comments.author: rmacklem
comments.body:
Currently, it ignores any RPCSEC_GSS context and maps it,
but I am fine with only AUTH_SYS and AUTH_NONE being
replaced by the squashing credentials.

I will simply patch the FreeBSD server, which is no problem
at this point in time.

comments.author: chucklever
comments.body:
Drafted with AI assistance under close review.

Fixed in 35f8ad824061. Identity squashing now applies to requests carrying an AUTH_NONE or AUTH_SYS credential. An RPCSEC_GSS request is processed under its GSS security context, per Section 4.2.1 of RFC 9289, with RFC 2203 added as a normative reference. The Session Binding claim is narrowed to squashed requests, and the GSSExportedName guidance now describes the no-keytab host use case.

One consequence not discussed here: the AUTH_TOOWEAK rejection from #5 takes the same scope, so an RPCSEC_GSS request on a session whose certificate identity cannot be applied still executes under its own context. Rick, does that match what you would expect the FreeBSD server to do once you patch it?

issues.title: A client cannot tell whether identity squashing was applied
issues.author: chucklever
issues.body:
Drafted with AI assistance from a review pass; quotes and citations verified against the source documents.

-03 §1.2 states the purpose of the mechanism as a restriction:

```
   This extension allows a
   server to restrict access from such a client to a single user
   identity, limiting exposure if that certificate is compromised.
```

§3.3 describes what happens when the restriction is not applied:

```
   RPC servers that do not implement this specification will not
   recognize the otherName OIDs defined in this document.  Such servers
   MUST ignore unrecognized otherName entries per Section 4.2.1.6 of
   [RFC5280].  These servers will process RPC requests using the
   credential information contained in the RPC header, subject to their
   normal authentication and authorization policies.
```

For AUTH_SYS the RPC header credential is client-asserted and unverified, so the outcome grants more privilege than the certificate would have: an administrator who issues squashing certificates believing access is confined to one identity gets, against such a server, whatever UID the client sends. -03 defines no way for a client to learn which regime is in force.

RFC 9289 §6.1.1 gives a second path to the same state:

```
   The initial AUTH_TLS probe occurs in cleartext.  An on-path attacker
   can alter a cleartext handshake to make it appear as though TLS
   support is not available on one or both peers.
```

RFC 9289 §6.1.1 offers client policies that mitigate the attack, and -03 requires neither of them. "downgrade", "fallback", "STRIPTLS" and "opportunistic" appear nowhere in the document.

Say that identity squashing requires a client policy that mandates TLS, and state what a client may assume when it cannot confirm the server applied the certificate identity. If no signal is possible, say so, and say that the failure is toward greater privilege.

comments.author: chucklever
comments.body:
Drafted with AI assistance; RFC 9289 quotations verified against the published text.

Rick's reply off-list (2026-08-21) covers the case where TLS succeeds and the server ignores the OID, and he is right that no in-band signal exists for it. The only server-to-client channel before the session is the AUTH_TLS probe reply, whose verifier carries the fixed "STARTTLS" token (Section 4.1 of RFC 9289). Signalling support there would update RFC 9289.

The STRIPTLS path is separate and needs no signal. Section 6.1.1 of RFC 9289 is advisory throughout: "Client implementers can choose from the following", and requiring a TLS session on every connection is "strongly encouraged". An on-path attacker can therefore turn a session that would have been squashed into a cleartext session in which the client asserts any UID it likes, and -03 forbids nothing about it.

Proposed resolution, three pieces of text:

1. A normative client requirement in Section 3: a client presenting a certificate that carries one of these otherName fields MUST use a security policy requiring a TLS session on every connection, and MUST NOT continue RPC operation in cleartext when the AUTH_TLS probe or the TLS handshake fails.

2. A Security Considerations subsection stating the failure direction: where the server does not implement this specification or does not authorize the asserted identity, the session proceeds under the RPC header credential, which for AUTH_SYS is asserted by the client and unverified. Absence of enforcement fails toward greater privilege.

3. A deployment statement in Section 3.3: issuing a certificate carrying these otherName fields is not itself a restriction. It restricts access only on servers that implement this specification, which is one reason Section 7.2.1 recommends separate trust anchors.

Rick's observation that a client cannot know whether the server maps root to an unprivileged identity stands, but that policy and server-side group lookup both fail toward lesser privilege, so the analogy does not reach this case.

One question for the WG on the first item. If this extension is read as governing only sessions that already reached TLS, the client requirement is vacuous, because a stripped session presents no certificate at all. The loss is not that the certificate goes unread; it is that the session proceeds under unrestricted AUTH_SYS when the certificate was meant to confine it.

comments.author: rmacklem
comments.body:
Normally, the FreeBSD server is configured to fail the
RPCs with weakauth when identity squashing is required
for either a non-TLS session or one where the X.509
cert. does not have an otherName that maps to a
user credential on the server.
(Would be for AUTH_SYS or AUTH_NONE, if you choose
to exempt RPCSEC_GSS.)

I've never thought of the case where identity squashing
is not required, but there is a TLS session where the X.509
certificate has an otherName field.
The alternatives seem to be..
1 - Fail all non-NULL RPCs with weakauth.
2 - Do the identity squashing.
3 - Ignore the otherName and don't do identity squashing.
Servers that do not know how to do identity squashing
will do #3, so maybe that is the preferred response when
identity squashing is not required by the server?
--> I think a server should either require it or ignore/not do it.

You could argue that, if a client wants to know if
identity squashing is required/being done, it can
try a TLS session without the cert. with a valid otherName
and see if "weakauth" is replied.

-

comments.author: chucklever
comments.body:
Drafted with AI assistance under close review.

Rick's require-or-ignore point is now in e61bdc70ffd5 as a Server Policy section. A server that implements this specification either enforces identity squashing or has it disabled, at a scope the server chooses. Disabled means ignore the otherName and behave as a non-supporting server, which a client cannot distinguish. Enforcing means AUTH_TOOWEAK on every non-NULL AUTH_NONE or AUTH_SYS request on a connection where no certificate identity was applied: no TLS session, no certificate, no squashing otherName, or an otherName the server cannot apply.

The no-TLS case is a MUST, so enforcing squashing on an export means refusing cleartext AUTH_SYS on it. That is what Rick describes FreeBSD doing when squashing is required, and it is what makes the client-side STRIPTLS requirement hold from the server side. Rick, is there a deployment where you would want squashing required and cleartext AUTH_SYS accepted on the same export? If so this should be a SHOULD.

The same commit fixes the Absence of Enforcement section, which said a server that does not authorize the identity falls back to the header credential. The AUTH_TOOWEAK rule forbids that, so it now names the disabled server as the one that falls through. Rick's probe, presenting a certificate with no squashing otherName and looking for AUTH_TOOWEAK, is noted there as the way a client confirms enforcement.

issues.title: RPCAuthSys has no effective GID field and no bound on the GID list
issues.author: chucklever

comments.author: chucklever
rmacklem
comments.body:
I would say that the "name@domain" maps to whatever the
server chooses. (I don't see any need to mention POSIX specifics?)

Something like "the name@domain is mapped to that user
identity on the server".

comments.author: chucklever
comments.body:
Drafted with AI assistance under close review.

Fixed in cf856fd07465 under the identity reading. RPCAuthSys names an identity in the terms AUTH_SYS uses and is not an AUTH_SYS credential, which is why stamp and machinename are absent. The first element of gids is the effective GID and the rest are supplementary. An empty list means the server supplies the groups from its own user database, which is what Rick describes the FreeBSD server doing for every form. The 16-element bound does not apply, since no wire credential is built. A server whose local representation cannot hold the whole list treats the identity as one it cannot apply rather than truncating it, so a certificate never silently confers a narrower identity than it names.

Rick's comment here answered the user@domain mapping question, which is now handled in #6. This issue was about the structure in the certificate, and FreeBSD has no code for this form, so the reading above is a choice rather than a description of running code. Objections welcome.

issues.title: Squashing assumes one RPC user per TLS session, and nothing establishes that
issues.author: chucklever
issues.body:
Drafted with AI assistance from a review pass; quotes and citations verified against the source documents.

-03 §1.2 quotes RFC 9289 §4.2 as the problem statement, including the sentence saying the property cannot be checked:

```
   When a client presents a TLS
   peer identity to an RPC server, the protocol extension described in
   the current document provides no way for the server to know whether
   that identity represents one RPC user on that client or is shared
   amongst many RPC users.
```

The mechanism is then specified without that condition attached. §7.3:

```
   All RPC operations within a TLS session containing an identity
   squashing otherName execute under the same user identity.
```

The justification for treating the property as satisfied is a deployment observation, in §1.2:

```
   Mobile devices such as laptops are typically used by a single user
   and do not have a fixed, well-known IP address or fully qualified DNS
   name.
```

Nothing turns the observation into a restriction on where the mechanism may be used.

RFC 9289 §6.2 describes the case the observation excludes:

```
   Moreover, client implementations are free to transmit RPC requests
   for more than one RPC user using the same TLS session.  Depending on
   the details of the client RPC implementation, this means that the
   client's TLS credentials are potentially visible to every RPC user
   that shares a TLS session.  Privileged users may also be able to
   access this TLS identity.
```

Under RFC 9289 alone, a local user who reaches the shared TLS credential still faces the server's per-user authorization. Under -03 that authorization is gone, since §3.2 step 6 discards the header credential: reaching the session is the whole of the authorization, and every request on it is attributed to the person named in the certificate.

Nothing in -03 obliges a client to restrict a squashed session to one RPC user. The normative requirements land on the server (§3.1, §7.2.1, §7.2.2, §7.2.3, §7.3, §7.4), and §5, which addresses CAs and administrators, opens "This section provides non-normative guidance". The party that knows whether it multiplexes RPC users onto one TLS session carries no obligation.

State normatively that a squashing certificate is presented only on a TLS session carrying a single RPC user, and say what a client owes before presenting one. If the mechanism is meant to apply to shared sessions too, say so, and say what the co-located user and the named account holder bear.

Related to #2.

comments.author: chucklever
comments.body:
Drafted with AI assistance.

Rick confirms off-list (2026-08-21) that one RPC user per TLS session is the intent: "Yes, it is one user per TLS session." He adds that the FreeBSD implementation was written for a personal device such as a laptop, where system and user are not distinct.

The confirmation settles the branch this issue left open. The mechanism is not meant to cover sessions carrying more than one RPC user, so the text to write is the normative restriction rather than a statement of what a co-located user and the named account holder bear.

The obligation belongs on the client, which is the party that knows whether it multiplexes RPC users onto one TLS session. The patch for #2 adds a Client Requirements section to §3 carrying client-side normative text, and the restriction belongs there: a client MUST NOT present a certificate carrying one of these otherName fields on a TLS session over which it transmits RPC requests for more than one RPC user.

Section 6.2 of RFC 9289 remains the reason to state it. A client that multiplexes exposes its TLS credential to every RPC user sharing the session, and under this extension reaching the session is the whole of the authorization.

comments.author: chucklever
comments.body:
Drafted with AI assistance under close review.

Fixed in 1874a67b1988, which adds a Client Requirements section: a client MUST NOT present a certificate carrying one of these otherName fields on a TLS session over which it transmits RPC requests for more than one RPC user. That is the normative restriction Rick's off-list confirmation of one user per session called for.

issues.title: The interoperability claim in §3.3 rests on a rule RFC 5280 §4.2.1.6 does not contain
issues.author: chucklever
issues.body:
Drafted with AI assistance from a review pass; quotes and citations verified against the source documents.

-03 §3.3:

```
   RPC servers that do not implement this specification will not
   recognize the otherName OIDs defined in this document.  Such servers
   MUST ignore unrecognized otherName entries per Section 4.2.1.6 of
   [RFC5280].  These servers will process RPC requests using the
   credential information contained in the RPC header, subject to their
   normal authentication and authorization policies.
```

RFC 5280 §4.2.1.6 states no such rule. Its entire treatment of otherName is:

```
   The subjectAltName MAY carry additional name types through the use of
   the otherName field.  The format and semantics of the name are
   indicated through the OBJECT IDENTIFIER in the type-id field.  The
   name itself is conveyed as value field in otherName.  For example,
   Kerberos [RFC4120] format names can be encoded into the otherName,
   using a Kerberos 5 principal name OID and a SEQUENCE of the Realm and
   the PrincipalName.
```

The nearest applicable rule is in RFC 5280 §4.2, and it operates on whole extensions rather than on GeneralName entries within one:

```
   A certificate-using system MUST reject the certificate if it encounters
   a critical extension it does not recognize or a critical extension
   that contains information that it cannot process.  A non-critical
   extension MAY be ignored if it is not recognized, but MUST be
   processed if it is recognized.
```

The "if it is not recognized" escape does not reach subjectAltName, which the same section lists as recognized:

```
   At a minimum, applications conforming to this profile MUST recognize
   the following extensions: key usage (Section 4.2.1.3), certificate
   policies (Section 4.2.1.4), subject alternative name (Section
   4.2.1.6),
```

RFC 5280 supplies no rule for an unknown type-id inside a recognized subjectAltName, so §3.3's fall-through is convention rather than an inherited requirement.

Criticality sharpens it for the deployment §1.2 describes. RFC 5280 §4.2.1.6:

```
   Further, if the only subject identity included in the certificate is
   an alternative name form (e.g., an electronic mail address), then the
   subject distinguished name MUST be empty (an empty sequence), and the
   subjectAltName extension MUST be present.  If the subject field
   contains an empty sequence, then the issuing CA MUST include a
   subjectAltName extension that is marked as critical.
```

A certificate whose only subject identity is the squashing otherName fits the laptop case in §1.2 and carries a critical subjectAltName. Whether a non-supporting server then rejects it turns on whether it judges that it "cannot process" the extension, which RFC 5280 does not settle. -03 says nothing about criticality anywhere; the only occurrence of "critical" in the document is §7.4's "timely revocation is critical".

Cite RFC 5280 §4.2 rather than §4.2.1.6, and say that GeneralName-level fall-through is convention rather than an inherited requirement. State the expected certificate profile: a non-empty subject DN and a non-critical subjectAltName, which RFC 5280 §4.2.1.6 already recommends where the subject DN is non-empty.

Related to #2.

comments.author: chucklever
comments.body:
Drafted with AI assistance; RFC 5280 and RFC 5531 text verified against the published RFCs.

Rick agrees off-list (2026-08-21) that the RFC 5280 reference can be dropped, and that requiring unrecognized OID values to be ignored is fine. He also proposes that a server which recognizes the OID but cannot map the identity to local credentials return AUTH_TOOWEAK to every non-NULL RPC on the session.

That second proposal is a signal, and it changes the conclusion reached in #2. Four outcomes, of which one is undetectable:

| Server | Outcome | What the client observes |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Recognizes the OID and authorizes the identity | requests squashed | nothing |
| Recognizes the OID, cannot map or authorize the identity | AUTH_TOOWEAK on non-NULL RPCs | the error |
| No support, non-critical subjectAltName | otherName ignored, header credential applies | nothing |
| No support, critical subjectAltName | rejection, or the row above; unspecified | handshake failure, or nothing |

Specifying the AUTH_TOOWEAK reply and pinning the certificate profile to a non-critical subjectAltName collapses the fourth row into the third. One undetectable case remains rather than three indistinguishable ones.

The profile fix is also a precondition for the text proposed in #2. That text says absence of enforcement falls through to the RPC header credential, which holds only once the fall-through is pinned. As -03 stands, a critical subjectAltName may instead lead a non-supporting server to reject the certificate. RFC 5280 does not settle which, and nothing elsewhere in it does: the only other treatment of "information that it cannot process" is §5.2, on CRL extensions.

Three pieces of text follow:

1. Cite RFC 5280 §4.2 rather than §4.2.1.6, and state the GeneralName-level fall-through as this document's own requirement rather than as an inherited one.

2. State the certificate profile: a non-empty subject distinguished name and a non-critical subjectAltName extension.

3. Specify the reply when the server recognizes the type-id but cannot map or authorize the identity: AUTH_TOOWEAK, which RFC 5531 defines as "rejected for security reasons", on every non-NULL procedure on that TLS session.

comments.author: rmacklem
comments.body:
As I noted in another comment, I think a server should either
require it or ignore it, since ignoring it is what servers that
do not implement squashing do now.

comments.author: chucklever
comments.body:
Drafted with AI assistance under close review.

Fixed in 0b9e42de0ac4. The interoperability section now cites Section 4.2 of RFC 5280 and states the GeneralName-level fall-through as this document's own requirement, requires a non-empty subject DN and a non-critical subjectAltName, and requires AUTH_TOOWEAK on every non-NULL procedure when the server recognizes the type-id but cannot apply the identity.

Rick's point that a server should either require squashing or ignore the otherName is about a server with the feature disabled, which the new text does not address. That is being carried in #2.

issues.title: Name canonicalization requirements point at RFC 8881 §5.9, which declines to specify them
issues.author: chucklever
issues.body:
Drafted with AI assistance from a review pass; quotes and citations verified against the source documents.

-03 §7.2.3.1, Name Canonicalization / NFSv4 Principals:

```
   When processing NFSv4Principal otherName values, servers MUST apply
   the same name canonicalization and domain validation procedures
   described in Section 5.9 of [RFC8881].  In particular:

   *  Domain names SHOULD be validated against expected domain suffixes

   *  Internationalized domain names MUST be properly normalized

   *  Case-sensitivity rules for usernames and domains MUST be
      consistently applied
```

RFC 8881 §5.9 describes no such procedures:

```
   The translation used to interpret owner and group strings is not
   specified as part of the protocol.  This allows various solutions to
   be employed.
```

The subordinate requirements have no referent either: -03 names no normalization form and states no case rules. Two conforming servers can canonicalize one certificate to two different local identities and authorize differently.

-03 also contradicts the section it points at. §3.6.2, Format of the otherName Value under NFSv4 User @ Domain String Identities:

```
   The otherName value contains an NFSv4Principal structure as defined
   in Appendix A, consisting of a UTF-8 encoded user name, the literal
   "@" character, and a UTF-8 encoded domain name, as described in
   Section 5.9 of [RFC8881].
```

Appendix B.6.3, Invalid Test Cases, requires that a string without "@" be rejected:

```
   Test Case 1: NFSv4Principal with missing '@' separator

   Input (malformed):

   *  principal: "aliceexample.com" (no '@' character present)

   Expected result: Rejection by server (invalid principal string
   format)
```

RFC 8881 §5.9 gives that string a defined meaning instead:

```
   In the case where there is no translation available to the client or
   server, the attribute value will be constructed without the "@".
   Therefore, the absence of the @ from the owner or owner_group
   attribute signifies that no translation was available at the sender
   and that the receiver of the attribute should not use that string as
   a basis for translation into its own internal format.
```

Name the normalization and case-folding rules directly rather than by reference to a section that declines to specify them, and reconcile the NFSv4 Format of the otherName Value subsection and Invalid Test Cases with RFC 8881 §5.9's meaning for a string without "@".

-02 carried a normative anchor here and -03 removed it. d7721364a099 removed a pointer to RFC 5280 §7.5 on correct grounds -- "The NFSv4Principal otherName carries a UTF-8 string and has no connection to rfc822Name encoding rules" -- reasoning that "The format is already described correctly in the following subsection, which cites RFC 8881 Section 5.9." That subsection is the NFSv4 Format of the otherName Value, and the RFC 8881 §5.9 citation is the one this issue is about.

Section numbers above are -03's. Patches pending for #2 and #5 insert new sections ahead of them, so the numbers shift in the next revision; the section names do not.

comments.author: chucklever
comments.body:
Drafted with AI assistance under close review; rfc8881bis-08 read directly, RFC 8881 quotations verified against the published text.

The reference target has moved. rfc8881bis-08 has no §5.9. The material is §17, Interpreting User and Group Designations, which says it "has been heavily revised from the version appearing in [RFC8881]". §17.1 keeps the sentence this issue turns on, verbatim:

```
   The translation used to interpret owner and group strings is not
   specified as part of the protocol.  This allows various solutions to
   be employed.
```

§17.2 goes further, calling the approach one that "left the common form undefined" and saying that "establishment of a common format was not possible". The first half of this issue holds against bis, and holds harder.

The second half does not. RFC 8881 §5.9's sentence giving a string with no "@" a defined meaning has no counterpart in bis-08. The contradiction between the NFSv4 Format of the otherName Value subsection (§3.6.2) and the Invalid Test Cases vector is an artifact of citing RFC 8881 rather than a defect in the mechanism.

Underneath both halves is a taxonomy problem. AUTH_SYS and RPCSEC_GSS credentials are RPC user identities. A user@domain string is not one: no RPC auth flavor carries it. §3.2 step 6 says the server replaces the credential information in the RPC header with the identity extracted from the certificate, which parses only when the certificate carries something that can occupy an RPC credential. For NFSv4Principal the server must resolve the string to a uid and gid set, or to a principal, before that step can run. -03 does not say so anywhere. §7.2.3.1 instead specifies that resolution as canonicalization requirements without admitting a resolution occurs, and the IANA table lists all three forms as peers.

Proposed direction, keeping all three forms: the certificate names an identity, and the server derives the RPC user from it. The derivation is trivial for RPCAuthSys and GSSExportedName. For NFSv4Principal it is the upper layer's own identity mapping, which confines the RFC 8881 dependency to that one step. §7.2.3.1 then drops its canonicalization bullets and requires instead that the server resolve the name through the same mapping it applies to the owner attribute, and deny when resolution fails. Splitting NFSv4Principal into a separate document would give a cleaner taxonomy, but would leave this document with two identity forms and no implementation.

Rick, two questions about the FreeBSD implementation. The answer decides whether that framing is right.

Does the server resolve the certificate's user@domain through NFSv4 idmapping to a uid and gid set and squash to that, or does it authorize against the string directly, the way an NFSv4 ACL who field is used?

If it resolves to a uid, what does the server do when the resolution fails?

comments.author: rmacklem
comments.body:
The FreeBSD server maps the "name@domain" to a uid, plus list of gids.
(It handles the "who" field of NFSv4 ACLs the same way, except Owner
is a uid and Group is a gid. In ZFS, the acl is stored with numeric uids and
gids, not strings.)

The same is also true of Kerberized NFS. The server maps the principal
name to what Kerberos calls an lname(), (For MIT's Kerberos implementation
I think it always just returns the same string?)
Then that is looked up in the password database and translated to a uid plus gid list.
--> All three do essentially the same thing.
(Dealing with a non-default "domain" is not supported.)

comments.author: chucklever
comments.body:
Drafted with AI assistance under close review.

Fixed in 45465439efb3, together with #7. The certificate names an identity and the server derives an RPC user from it when the TLS session is established. For NFSv4Principal the derivation is resolution through the server's NFSv4 owner mapping, which RFC 8881 leaves to the implementation, so the canonicalization bullets are gone and the section is now Name Resolution. A string the mapping cannot resolve is an identity the server cannot apply, which routes to AUTH_TOOWEAK. The format subsection requires the "@" character and says why RFC 8881's meaning for its absence does not apply to a certificate, and it carries the note that a server whose mapping ignores the domain resolves only its own.

The GSSExportedName section gained a parallel requirement: derive the RPC user as the server does from an RPCSEC_GSS principal under the same mechanism. That follows Rick's description of the lname path.

A follow-up in a4750c70cddf points out that the user@domain form names an NFSv4 identity rather than an RPC one, since resolving it needs an owner mapping that only an NFSv4 server has. The format guidance no longer recommends it for heterogeneous environments. Rick, that reads as a layering observation to me. Do you see a non-NFS RPC server ever resolving user@domain? If so the form is generic and that commit should come out.

issues.title: Credential replacement is possible for only one of the three identity forms
issues.author: chucklever
issues.body:
Drafted with AI assistance under close review; RFC 2203 and RFC 5531 structures verified against the published text.

-03 §3 states the mechanism as credential replacement:

```
   The receiving system (an RPC server) then
   replaces the RPC user, as carried in the RPC header credential and
   verifier fields in each RPC request within the TLS session, with the
   user identity specified in the certificate used to authenticate that
   session.
```

§3.2 step 6 repeats it:

```
   6.  For each incoming RPC request on this TLS session, replace the
       credential information in the RPC header with the identity
       extracted from the certificate.  The original credential
       information in the RPC header is ignored.
```

Replacement is possible for one of the three identity forms. AUTH_SYS is a credential the certificate can reproduce: RFC 5531 Appendix A defines authsys_parms as stamp, machinename, uid, gid, and gids, and RPCAuthSys carries the uid and a group list.

The other two forms are names. Section 5.1 of RFC 2203 defines the RPCSEC_GSS credential:

```
              struct {
                  rpc_gss_proc_t gss_proc;  /* control procedure */
                  unsigned int seq_num;   /* sequence number */
                  rpc_gss_service_t service; /* service used */
                  opaque handle<>;       /* context handle */
              } rpc_gss_cred_vers_1_t;
```

The principal appears nowhere in it. A GSS name is established during context creation and held in server-side context state, so a certificate can name the principal but cannot supply what the credential carries. An NFSv4 user@domain string is not an RPC credential in any flavor; it is an upper-layer name that RFC 8881 leaves to a translation the protocol does not specify.

The ASN.1 module in Appendix A already reflects this. RPCAuthSys carries credential fields, while GSSExportedName carries a mechanism OID and a name value, and NFSv4Principal carries a UTF8String. Two of the three are names by construction. Only the prose treats the three as peers.

The verifier makes it plainer. -03 says the server replaces "the RPC header credential and verifier fields". For AUTH_SYS the verifier is AUTH_NONE and there is nothing to replace. For RPCSEC_GSS the verifier is a MIC computed over the header under the established context, which a certificate cannot produce.

What a server can actually do with GSSExportedName or NFSv4Principal is resolve the name to a local identity and execute the session's requests under it. -03 never says a resolution occurs. §7.2.3.1 instead specifies the NFSv4 resolution as canonicalization requirements, which is how that section came to demand procedures RFC 8881 declines to supply (#6).

State the mechanism as naming and derivation rather than replacement: the certificate names an identity, and the server derives the RPC user from it. The derivation is direct for RPCAuthSys, and is a name resolution for the other two forms. Say what a server does when resolution fails, and drop the claim that the verifier is replaced.

Related to #1 and #6.

comments.author: chucklever
comments.body:
Drafted with AI assistance under close review.

Fixed in 45465439efb3 together with #6. The mechanism section now states naming and derivation rather than replacement, the verifier claim is gone, and the derivation is given per form: direct for RPCAuthSys, the server's principal mapping for GSSExportedName, the NFSv4 owner mapping for NFSv4Principal. A failed derivation routes to the AUTH_TOOWEAK rule.
